name: Reed Yellow
lede: Reed Yellow is a warm, muted gold, named for the plant and recorded as early as 1530 by Maerz and Paul.

sections.title: An old name for a warm gold
sections.body:
Maerz and Paul's 1930 dictionary gives Reed Yellow a first recorded date of 1530, at plate 11 E 2, far earlier than most names in our library [1]. Ridgway's 1912 nomenclature separately places it at plate XXX, hue 23'', tone b, and the ISCC-NBS system of 1955 files it as block 101, a light greenish yellow [1]. Werner's 1821 nomenclature, which ties each color to natural comparisons, pairs this hue with the body of the silk moth, white currants and Saxon topaz [1].

The nearest named color is [[sunbeam|Sunbeam]], 2.5 units away and a shade brighter; [[baryta-yellow|Baryta Yellow]] sits 2.8 units off, paler [2]. [[maple|Maple]] is 3.5 units away, and [[colonial-buff|Colonial Buff]] is 3.7 units off [2]. In LCH terms Reed Yellow measures lightness 80, chroma 39, hue 92 degrees [2].

sections.title: Field notes
sections.body: Our archive finds Reed Yellow in 991 of 23,781 paintings, 4.17 percent, as photographed, more common than 87 percent of the archive's named colors [3]. It peaks in the 1400s, in 35 of 945 paintings, at 1.2 times the expected rate for that century, and Adolphe Joseph Thomas Monticelli is its most devoted painter, present in 5 of his 22 works here at 4.1 times his baseline [3]. It most often turns up as an accent, in 52 percent of its paintings, rather than as a shadow [3]. The earliest match is dated 1230, five hundred ninety-one years before Werner's 1821 record of the name — a look-alike hue in an aged photograph, not proof of the dye or pigment itself, a floor and not a first, since the archive's early centuries are thin [3].
